title: Creating as you go and playing the same solo nightly
summary: Caldwell does not remember what he played the night before; arranged parts repeat, while free numbers change each night, as in Copenhagen.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: No, because I've found out two things Stanley (unintelligible) that, what the guys used to say to (unintelligible) me, said, you know, you a funny man with the horn. I said why. Said, we hear you play one night the same thing, and we go back the next night you don't -- what, did you forget what you played the night before? I says, I don't remember what I played the day before, because I'm always thinking about something else.

And Hawks said, well, you create as you go along, don't you? I said, well, maybe that's what you call it. But like he wrote in that book about those nine different choruses. I wasn't there and practicing on nine different choruses. I made the -- made two or three bars like so. Forget about it.
But when you get on -- the band is behind you, and you get that feeling, and they create.

Well, I take it, though, that if you -- I mean if you had an arrangement for a band and you played with this band every night, and you also have to fit that arrangement, then your solo is going to become rather the same every night.
It will because you are accustomed to playing it, and it comes.
You know you've got to make it fit with the --

-- what the -- when the brass is -- well, that's one thing, but if you play for, say, you know, some jump number with a totally different band six nights running, you'd probably take a different solo (unintelligible).
Oh, that's what happened with me over there in Copenhagen, because they'd ask you. I'd say
anything you fellows want to play. Well, they'd play all them swing tunes, this and that, ballads (unintelligible). It was real nice with me.
